Upon performing zero-field cooling, followed by a magnetization measurement, we noticed a characteristic under-curve or under-hysteresis shape in the obtained magnetization curves, a phenomenon that can be attributed to the presence of ferromagnetic clusters in an overall paramagnetic matrix. Our findings for x ≈ 0.6 further show a remarkable temperature and field stability of the freezing temperature, a characteristic that aligns with a mean-field type of spin freezing mechanism. Upon conducting a muon spin relaxation measurement, we discovered a significant enhancement in the transverse field μ+SR relaxation rate, τ^{-1}_p, for the composition x = 0.67 at temperatures above 2 K, thereby providing direct evidence for the presence of slow-spin fluctuations in the system. Our study further indicates that the origin of the observed neutron depolarization for the respective compositions can be attributed to the emergence of ferrom

Using the Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical Telescope, 19-beam observations of the 21-cm line toward the high-mass star-forming region G176.51+00.20 were carried out. The data showed complex and possibly complex-shaped structures associated with associated molecular cloud complexes, particularly in relation to two diffuse HI components. These components, one of which likely passes through the Sgr disk, exhibit narrow-line widths and self-absorption. These self-absorptions are spatially localized and correlated with the critical density isothermal molecular cloud structures. These self-absorptions are estimated to be at most 1.7 pc from the cloud edges. These findings imply that the interstellar medium at the high end of the Galactic disk transverse velocity range is associated with the cloud complexes, and also reveal hints of related HI self-absorptions within the molecular cloud structures, which may be related to cloud internal flows.

We demonstrate the topological equivalence of all intermediate beta-transformations with a specific type of greedy beta-transformation that incorporates a hole at zero. By employing this equivalence, we obtain a detailed characterization of these transformations, yielding new insights and results in various areas, such as Krieger embeddings, survivor sets, Hausdorff dimensions, bifurcation sets, and badly approximable numbers. We show that certain classes of sets associated with these beta-transformations possess unique properties, specifically that they are winning in Schmidt games and have the countable intersection property.

Determining the CP-violating phase phi_s resulting from mixing-induced phenomena in Bs decays is a crucial method for discovering potential new physics phenomena. Utilizing approximately 7,421 +/- 105 signal events from predominantly CP-odd final states (J/\psi pi+ pi-), which were isolated in 1/fb of pp collision data gathered at a 7 TeV energy level by the LHCb detector, researchers performed a time-dependent analysis on the obtained data. As a result, phi_s was estimated to be -0.019 +/- 0.173 +/- 0.004 radians, in alignment with the Standard Model predictions. Furthermore, their findings revealed no indication of direct CP violation.

It's astonishing that deep deep neural networks, despite being designed to learn patterns, frequently fail in real-world scenarios due to differences between training and actual data. Notably, this issue arises from disparate environments, where data may differ substantially. Unlike the vast amount of labeled data available for training, there's a shortage of labeled data in scenarios where networks are deployed in real-world settings. As a result, there's an evident need for models that can seamlessly adapt to new domains with minimal labeled data. To bridge this gap, domain adaptation has emerged as a technique to address this concern. This work focuses on evaluating domain adaptation approaches for image classification, analyzing four primary techniques: deep domain confusion, class weight alignment, representation learning, and adversarial training. Furthermore, we examined methods of labeled data enhancement, including re-weighting, and combined these with three types of unlabeled data processing methods. Our experiments revealed that a straightforward yet efficient yet efficient yet efficient yet efficient yet efficient approach, involving re-weighting of labeled data and random processing of unlabeled data, yielded superior results, consistently performing better than more complex techniques across four datasets. Notably, our method, dubbed DAIL, surpassed state-of-the-art results without requiring any parameter optimization, consistently achieving generalization.

In finite fields of dimension 2, an arc is a subset where no 3 points share a line. To determine the total number of such arcs, a specific counting method, called hypergraph counting, is employed with the restriction that no 3 points form a line. A particular inequality regarding the counting of these arcs in finite fields of dimension 2 can be shown through induction as the dimension increases.

A pictorial proof shows that there are $\binom{n+2}{4}$ equilateral triangles in a regular $n$-sided triangle by establishing a one-to-one correspondence between four-element subsets of the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n+2\}$ and the equilateral triangles in this grid, where it is visually represented by illustrating the triangle corresponding to the subset $\{4, 5, 8, 11\}$ when $n$ is $10$.

Despite recent advancements in Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), explaining their predictive decisions remains an unresolved issue. Current methods primarily address the interpretation of individual cases (i.e., important graph structures and node attributes) to understand model predictions, but generate instance-specific explanations that fail to provide a broader understanding of the GNN model, restricting their general applicability in the inductive setting. Moreover, these methods struggle to provide natural explanations for groups of cases (e.g., graphs of the same class). To address these limitations, this study proposes a parameterized explainer for GNNs, capable of generating a continuous spectrum of explanations for an input graph from irrelevant to relevant, reflecting the model's confidence in its prediction. Experimental results demonstrate the benefits of our approach, showcasing more effective and generalizable explanations for object detection tasks on various benchmarks.

The peculiar system, RXCJ0232.2-4420, at $z$ = 0.28, contains a unique radio halo surrounding its central cluster core. To explore its development and composition, we examined archival X-ray data from Chandra and XMM-Newton, examining the dynamic cluster state and searching for gas substructures. Its X-ray brightness distribution exhibits no evident disruption except for an elongation in the North-East to South-West direction. We applied the unsharp masking technique and calculated the morphology parameters to assess disturbance levels. These analyses identified a South-West substructure located at approximately 1 arcminute from the core, indicating the system may possess a quiet core but turbulent surroundings that potentially pump energy to the detected radio halo.

Recently, the Legendre Memory Unit (LMU), a novel type of recurrent neural network, was developed and has demonstrated superior performance on various benchmark datasets. In this work, the linear component of the LMU is optimized, resulting in a simplified variant that can be trained in parallel, thus overcoming the obstacle of GPU training limitations. Our modified LMU variant is compatible with existing RNN architectures, offering a practical solution for large-scale networks. Furthermore, the LMU's performance is enhanced by training it concurrently with the accompanying RNN. Our experiments show that the LMU's predictive capabilities are notably better when trained separately, and the proposed architecture allows for efficient training on high-performance GPUs. We showcase the effectiveness of the LMU variant by achieving state-of-the-art results on 50-digit arithmetic and the 10-digit TST.

As the next decade unfolds, the field of particle physics is driven to unravel the enigma of dark matter, the universe's imbalance of matter over antimatter, the seemingly calculated balance of the electro-weak scale, and unusual phenomena at high altitudes observed by TeV particles. To address these long-standing questions, it is anticipated that new and innovative experimental methods will be required. This report outlines various potential areas to explore, where early attempts are underway or show great promise, including the possibility of introducing "portable" detectors to enhance the sensitivity of sensitive experiments and their implications.

Language plays a vital role in a society, and factors contributing to its emergence and progression remain areas of contemporary research focus. Previous studies on the naming game, which includes work by Girard and Piaget, have shown that a consistent system of language can arise from diverse, randomly selected initial options. However, when agent correspondence principles are not strictly adhered to, challenges arise, particularly when agent names no longer match their inherent characteristics. This paper delves into the naming game with dynamic correspondences, where agents are free to move and name assignments can result in miscommunication, causing them to change their names. A theoretical analysis of the equation for this system is provided, along with an empirical examination of a range of corresponding principles. The findings show that, regardless of the principle governing correspondence, the results conform to a general pattern of exponential growth over time, characterized by a characteristic time based on the total characteristics and the number of possible names. Ultimately, it is shown that, in the naming game with dynamic correspondences, a consistent system of language is guaranteed to emerge over time.

PINN algorithms have made significant breakthroughs in solving various complex PDE-based problems. Despite these achievements, they often struggle to achieve optimal convergence when the target function contains intricate details. By leveraging the properties of neural tangent kernels, we have investigated how PINNs train under a momentum-based stochastic gradient descent. Our findings indicate that incorporating momentum substantially diminishes the impact of spectral bias, leading to better convergence. Additionally, we discovered that using the Adam optimizer not only introduces momentum-related benefits but also regulates the exploration-exploitation trade-off more effectively than conventional gradient descent. Our experiments further validate that using larger networks with momentum-based optimization leads to improved convergence even for target functions with high frequencies.

We examine a two-wave system in the interval (-1,1), where one wave absorbs energy and the other does not, with partial damping that is also locally applied. This model has been modified from the Kelvin-Voigt damping model by adding an arbitrarily small amount of noise, or viscoelasticity. Using the uniformly boundedness principle and the Dainella-Leugering theorem, we find that the model behaves stably under certain conditions involving the viscoelasticity coefficients and wave propagation speeds. This study expands the work of Leugering et al. and Dassios et al. and addresses an issue left open in a prior investigation by Chueshov and Lasiecka.

Recent advances in deep reinforcement learning have led to widespread success across various applications, yet deep RL methods struggle with two key limitations: efficiency and transparency. The high efficiency of general deep RL methods comes at the cost of poor task adaptation, whereas rule-based methods excel in task adaptation but suffer from poor efficiency. The lack of transparency in deep RL methods makes it difficult to understand the reasoning behind the agents' actions. To address these challenges, we propose a novel hierarchical framework that combines the efficiency of deep RL methods and the adaptability of rule-based methods, accompanied by intuitive explanations. The framework assumes that reward functions can be learned through the analysis of underlying rules, allowing the derivation of interpretable state and action models. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed framework effectively identifies relevant features, accurately replicates reward models, and achieves better performance compared to baseline methods.

We've developed an all-optical technique for producing optical nonreciprocity on a microchip, achieved through the process of quantum squeezing a specific mode in coupled resonator systems. A key factor in this method involves applying classical coherent light in a one-way fashion to parametrically pump a nonlinear resonator. This selective pumping induces a chiral interaction between photons within the resonators, allowing us to build optical diodes and quasi-circulators. Notably, we've demonstrated the functionality of these nonreciprocal devices even with weak input, using a combination of squeezed-vacuum fields and classical pump light. We observed isolation ratios greater than 40 dB in optical diodes, as well as a high fidelity rate for quasi-circulators. We also found that our method allows for low-loss optical communication. Furthermore, we've demonstrated the ability to control the flow of light through our system using a relatively weak control light, effectively enabling the development of nonreciprocal optical transistors.

We expand upon the research initiated by P. Fenton by analyzing a function that sums translates, defined as $T(f):=\sum_{1\leq j\0} h_j ( Tf_{j} ) ( z )$, where $T$ is an $L^p$ multiplier operator for $1 < p < \infty$, and $f=\{f_j\}_{j=1}^0$ consists of scalar-valued functions within the specified $L^p$ space. Our investigation focuses on the minimax and maximax problems associated with the expression $\inf_{f\in F} \sup_{1\leq j\0} \| Tf_j\|_{L^q(z)}$ with $q>2$, ultimately yielding minimax identities reminiscent of Fenton's classic result. Our research introduces an innovative technique by incorporating $L^p$ multipliers and functional-Lorentz spaces into the analysis.

The CRESST experiment is one of the leading projects for directly detecting dark matter particles weighing less than GeV/c$^2$. Its ability to analyze numerous isotopes within its target material is an advantage in exploring dark matter interactions. This research focuses on dark matter interactions with $^{6}$Li protons and neutrons, made feasible through updated nuclear matrix calculations for this specific lithium isotope. By utilizing data collected by a CRESST prototype using LiAlO$_2$ and tested above ground in Munich, Germany, we demonstrate the effectiveness of incorporating $^{6}$Li into our calculations to improve our detection of spin-dependent interactions between dark matter and neutrons, particularly beneficial for particles weighing less than 1 GeV/c$^2$ where significant improvements are found.

Blind Image deblurring attempts to estimate a latent image's sharpness and a blurred image, an ill-posed problem, resolved by restricting either the image or a blur kernel representing blur. Differing from prior research, this study regulates the structure of the blur kernel. The kernel mixture concept utilizes Gaussian kernels with enhanced scale and center configurations, producing a nearly non-parametric blur shape representation. The decision of the base kernel count becomes more flexible due to a data-driven method. This strategy is successfully tested in a satellite imaging scenario where it outperforms current standards regulating latent images in favour of the kernel's structural adjustment.

This paper introduces a new concept called associative BiHom-Yang-Baxter pair with weight (λ,γ) which can be used to solve the double curved Rota-Baxter BiHom-Yang-Baxter equation. Furthermore, we establish equivalent definitions of covariant BiHom-bialgebra with quasitriangular properties and show that the BiHom-Yang-Baxter equation of weight -1 can be derived from a unitary quasitriangular covariant BiHom-bialgebra. Lastly, we outline two methods for constructing BiHom-pre-Lie modules from Rota-Baxter BiHom-Yang-Baxter equation solutions.

Formal verification offers mathematically certain outcomes, but the process is
typically hampered by the requirement for precise formal specifications,
hard to derive directly from natural language instructions given in development
environments. This research proposes a novel approach to formalizing program
properties, grounded in the assumption that all essential properties of a
program are extractable from its formal requirements. To accomplish this, we
leverage natural language specifications, link them to logical structures via
a meaning model drawing on (i) Montague's logical forms, (ii) the BBNF
description system, and (iii) the SMT solver, Z3. Our method iteratively
checks a property's validity and, if it fails, instantly detects and resolves
any inconsistencies. This newly designed methodology is demonstrated by
achieving formal verification of two non-trivial, real-world Hoare logic
properties from their respective Java code and natural language descriptions.

Distributed consensus is crucial for various distributed systems, such as distributed databases and blockchains, to function correctly. The Canopus protocol efficiently manages large-scale distributed consensus without the need for a single leader, achieving this through a virtual tree structure that limits network traffic and hardware redundancies within the network. The existing Canopus protocol excels at performance but excels at failure resilience, therefore we introduce RCanopus, a modification designed to handle failures more effectively and enhance fault tolerance. Compared to current consensus protocols, RCanopus surpasses many rival protocols such as Pq-JFT and PqLC, while performing similarly or better than the Terrier protocol, especially under heavy system loads, despite statistical inaccuracy under certain network conditions.

Recent studies utilizing neutron spin echo and nuclear magnetic resonance relaxation methods, which examine linear transport properties, have yielded contrasting results when analyzing the impact of cholesterol on the bending modulus of lipid bilayers. This inconsistency arose despite earlier research employing solely equilibrium experiments, not linear transport properties, indicating that one may be misled by data from the latter. A general discussion highlights how this misunderstanding occurs, after which it's demonstrated that the neutron spin echo findings can be reinterpreted to be consistent with the prior equilibrium results, thereby resolving the disparity. Furthermore, in the context of nuclear magnetic resonance relaxation methods, there exists confusion over which property this measure represents; specifically, it's related to the bilayer's compression modulus.

This paper examines the loop quantum cosmological model generated from the ADM Hamiltonian of a minimally coupled cosmological scalar field. Similar to previous studies on the loop quantum cosmology derived from the Einstein-Hilbert action, we have found support for the bounces predicted at the cosmological singularity. Furthermore, our model aligns with the loop quantum cosmological models based on the ADM Hamiltonian of the Einstein-Hilbert action in certain aspects, yet it also differs in other aspects. It was also revealed that the loop quantum cosmological models derived from the total Hamiltonian and the Hamiltonian of the spatial component exhibit distinct features.

The Pierre Auger Observatory catalog details 100 extensive air-showers 
recorded between 2004 and 2020 for high-energy particles, spanning a specific
energy range from 78 to 166 EeV. This comprehensive dataset is made available 
for close examination, alongside nine events used to establish the energy scale 
for each detected primary particle. An accompanying plot displays the locations 
where these energetic particles entered Earth's atmosphere, leaving their data unanalyzed.

Incorporating deep neural networks into robotic systems poses a significant problem 
due to the lack of reliable measures for their output predictions. Probabilistic 
machine learning frameworks offer an answer to this issue by attributing a likelihood 
distribution to classification and localisation results. Despite some object detectors 
utilising probability output for predictions, this approach fails to account for the 
limited accuracy of object boundaries and encompassing areas. To resolve this issue, 
this research presents BayesOD, a pioneering framework for estimating uncertainty 
in object detection by integrating Bayesian inference with existing pipelines. By 
utilising a predefined understanding of the likelihood of object presence and likelihood 
of background, the method integrates these inputs into a clear probability map. 
Results from our method show consistent improvement over other existing uncertainty 
estimation techniques for object detectors, as demonstrated on PASCAL VOC and COCO 
datasets. Furthermore, the associated code is accessible via github at the link 
https://github.com/asharakeh/BayesOD.

The integration of advanced traffic forecasting technology significantly affects urban transportation systems, enabling more accurate trip planning and resource allocation. The TFSys platform, a city-wide data collection and decision support system, relies on the traffic forecasting component, known as Traffic Forecasting on Traffic Snippets (TFS), to provide accurate predictions within a city's transportation network. The TFS approach leverages machine learning to train a user-friendly interface for automated traffic forecasting. The performance and adaptability of TFS have been demonstrated through testing on a network of locations within Chicago, with promising results. The implementation of TFS within the city's system has been successfully deployed and is currently in operational use.

In recent years, rewriting theory has been used to create systematic approaches to proving coherence in strict higher categories. We're taking this theory further by applying it to Gray categories, which can be thought of as a specific type of tricategory. To achieve this, we need to adapt rewriting theory to the context of precategories, which encompasses Gray categories, and allows for automated calculations. Our findings demonstrate that precategories with a finite rewriting system have a limited number of critical interactions that can be quickly calculated. We also broadened the scope of Squier's theorem to fit our research framework, which led us to the discovery that convergent rewriting systems lead to coherence in Gray categories, implying that equivalent parallel transformations can be proven identical through a finite series of transformations. This led to significant advancements in the field, including proving the categorification, tricategorification, and 4-categorification of the coherence theorems related to Gray monoids, symmetric categories, commutative intensifiers, commutative categories, commutative 2-categories, commutative procategories, commutative quasi-categories, commutative globular categories, and monoidal categories.

Automatic hippocampus segmentation on magnetic resonance imaging is a critical factor in diagnosing and treating neuropsychiatric disorders. Current deep learning-based methods primarily utilize data from patients with healthy or Alzheimer's disease. This raises concerns about performance gaps in other domains, such as patients with epilepsy and hippocampal resections. This study investigated the application of hippocampus segmentation using Conv3D-NET, HippoNet, and AutoNet deep networks, which were previously trained on auto-segmentation pipelines. The results demonstrate that these networks can provide accurate hippocampal segmentation in various domains, including epilepsy and malformations.

We scrutinize an experiment claiming to showcase the quantum pigeonhole effect by having three parties navigate a two-path interferometer with no pair of them using the same path simultaneously. Through an analysis based on weak values, we uncover inconsistencies in the description. By incorporating transversal modes and examining the emergence of correlations between path and traversal properties, we also investigate the rotational symmetry of the output pattern as an indicator of pairwise interactions. However, our analysis finds that the symmetry bears no evident connection to the probability of three particles exiting the interferometer together.

This research investigates the concentration of cosmic ray albedo neutrons albedo protons (CRAND) trapped within the Earth's and magnetic field, focusing specifically on protons produced near the Earth's equatorial regions, which are then captured by the planet's magnetic field and transported towards the poles. The, in this study, the distribution of these captured protons in low Earth orbit is examined using a Monte Carlo method, which takes into account spatial and temporal variations of galactic cosmic ray flux, as well as effects due to the Earth's magnetic field. The model employed in this research draws upon previous modeling of galactic cosmic ray distributions in the Earth's atmosphere, utilizing a cutoff rigidity dependent exponential for the radial variation and a latitude-dependent exponential for the magnetic field's curvature, while maintaining the original energy distribution of the neutrons and protons. Additionally, this research considers the, in this study, the Earth's magnetic field is examined through a numerical integration of the Shocks, in this research, the Shocks model (Gleeson and Strong 1991) which depends on the local magnetic field's strength and temperature for the radial variation and a exponential for the polar radius of the galactic disk. The research's results, which show the relationship between the trapped proton and neutron flux and the cosmic ray energy, are compared to observations at the Earth's orbit.

A network's expressivity is a crucial factor in assessing deep neural networks, 
as it correlates directly with the limitations of achievable performance gains. This 
paper proposes a novel three-phase training approach based on expressivity 
criteria, consisting of global model reduction, weight refinement, and architecture 
redesign through link reconfiguration. In the initial phase, a global model 
shrinking method is applied to mitigate overfitting and promote transferable 
representations. Subsequently, weight refinement is performed to maximize 
model weights' expressivity. Finally, a topology assessment tool is used to 
identify underutilized connections, which are then reestablished to maintain 
network connectivity. This process is referred to as Deep GNN architecture design 
with expressivity phases, offering a 6% relative improvement over conventional GNN 
architectures on 10 industries, including chemical, bio, and text processing.

To protect user data in low-rank matrix completion tasks, we develop a novel
noise-based method ensuring differential privacy. This method incorporates
noise with characteristics inspired by the Huber loss function in robust
statistics, and is termed as the Huber mechanism. In our study, we evaluate the
performance of this Huber mechanism against other privacy mechanisms, including
using the Alternating Least Squares method to solve matrix completion tasks.
Furthermore, we apply the Iteratively Re-Weighted Least Squares algorithm and
investigate how different noise-based approaches function in this method. Our
results demonstrate the Huber mechanism's efficacy, particularly when dealing
with low-rank matrix completion, and highlight its ability to fill in accurately
missing data values while maintaining data privacy.

We propose a novel approach to modelling interstellar dust where larger grains are comprised of a uniform material, referred to as 'astrodust', and tiny particles, known as PAHs, come in various distinct forms. The evidence suggests that a uniform grain composition is most consistent with the observed patterns of infrared polarization, and the established ratio between optical and infrared polarization. A detailed analysis reveals that a combination of astrodust and PAHs accurately replicates the properties of galactic extinction and emission from interstellar dust while adhering to existing constraints on dust abundance. The associated data and software have been made publicly accessible for further research.

Research using the ALMA telescope has revealed distinct substructures in the circumstellar discs surrounding very low-mass stars. A significant number of such stars have been found to have linearly arranged spiral structures resembling a ring, exemplified by the spiral structure around CIDA 1. This study aimed to determine the cause of the spiral structure around CIDA 1 by using various radial density models, leading to the discovery that a massive Jupiter-like planet, with an estimated mass between 0.035-0.192 M Jupiter, is necessary to explain the observed pattern. Furthermore, it was found that the planet's influence could have originated from either the planet's initial formation location or its current position, resulting in the overstimulation of the surrounding material and the transfer of its angular momentum. A massive planet in the protoplanetary disc or the early moving planet process has been found to be the most plausible explanation for the spiral structure in the disc around CIDA 1.

Given a set of click locations, \{($a_1$,$b_1$), \ldots, ($a_n$,$b_n$)\}, with each location randomly selected from the grid $[1..m]\times[1..m]$, we study the expected largest click count, denoted as $\mathcal{E}(\mathbb{S}_m^2)$, where the expected largest click count on the grid $[1..m]\times[1..m]$ is given by the average outcome of turning off all lights off by clicking at all the given set of click locations. It's also given in the paper that $\mathcal{E}(\mathbb{S}_m^2)$ behaves additively with respect to the size of the grid $[1..m]\times[1..m]$, with the result being $\frac{6m^5}{73}+O(m^4)$, where $m$ is arbitrarily large. This problem is also given as an open problem in the past paper $\mathbb{S}_m^1$. The result obtained here will be used in future work to compute the exact distribution of the largest click count, with the result obtained at click count out to 8, with the result obtained that $\mathcal{E}(\mathbb{S}_8^2)$ is equal to 2906.

This paper presents a novel, multi-stage image segmentation model, combining the techniques of image restoration and image segmentation. The integration of image restoration aspects enables the proposed model to effectively handle images corrupted by noise, blurriness, missing pixels, and varied illumination conditions. Specifically, we developed a two-stage approach that uses the Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to remove image noise and enhance its overall quality, followed by a variational segmentation model that uses the refined image quality to produce accurate segmentations. Experimental results demonstrate the proposed model's ability to accurately analyze medical images, while also showcasing its flexibility to apply to images from diverse domains such as space and natural image analysis.

Program analysis through Abstract Interpretation involves simulating the behavior of a program in a simplified environment to approximate its true behavior. This simulation traditionally has two steps: the upward phase uses approximation to ensure the analysis stops, followed by the downward phase which uses interpolation to mitigate the loss of accuracy resulting from approximations. This paper suggests an alternative by temporarily switching from an initial approximation to a more precise one, before applying the interpolation phase to improve overall accuracy. The proposed approach is theoretically justified and tested on a simple case study, which yielded substantial gains in precision for several different scenarios.

A broad range of structural phases in perovskite oxides host various physical properties that contribute to a variety of technological applications. Topological phonons, encompassing nodal rings, lines, and points, are found in different oxide perovskite systems, including structural forms (tetragonal, orthorhombic, rhombohedral), and intermediate stages between them. These topological phonons are found not only in stable structural forms but also in intermediate stages, and exemplified by the tetragonal-orthorhombic intermediate state of strontium titanate. External stimuli, such as electron irradiation, and illumination by ultraviolet light and magnetic fields, control the evolution of topological phonons. Consequently, the application of hybrid quantum matter based on oxide perovskite systems, especially their hybrid quantum topological phonons, presents great promise for future technological advancements.

Unsupervised outlier detection in various fields such as data mining and machine learning relies heavily on distance-based methods due to their adaptability in generic metric spaces. Large real-world data sets demand efficient algorithms able to detect outliers quickly, regardless of space dimension. Presently utilized approaches often suffer from limitations, either having a high computational complexity or depending on specific data types or dimensions. Advanced algorithms, like those based on graph analysis, can offer precise outcomes but are typically suited to specific data sets or dimensions. Our novel method can effectively detect outliers in any type of generic metric space, focusing on proximity graphs and unveiling the hidden connection between graph centrality measures and outlier detection outcomes. Our experimental findings demonstrate that this method rivals the performance of contemporary algorithms.

The probability of (de-)excitation and photon emission is evaluated for a non-relativistic, moving atom interacting with a quantum electromagnetic field near a stationary, perfectly conducting plane. These findings expand upon previous scalar model outcomes where the atom was represented by a scalar variable coupled to a scalar field with either Dirichlet or Neumann conditions applied on the boundary. This assessment considers how spontaneous emission rates change when an initially excited atom is accelerated versus an atom at rest encountering a moving mirror.

As applications relying on graph representations grow, the focus has shifted from global fairness to incorporating fairness at the node level, considering that Graph Neural Network (GNN)-based models operate within a local data framework. A novel framework, called Local Neighborhood Fairness (LNF), is introduced to capture fairness in data labeled by GNNs, where the concept of neighborhood is defined as a subset of nodes associated with each instance. Experimental results, derived from the FairGraph benchmark, are provided to support LNF, showing that it enhances both test accuracy and fairness for 14 out of 16 evaluated datasets. Additionally, it is demonstrated that LNF is a more sensitive metric than existing fairness standards as it is more strongly correlated with model performance. A comprehensive study of LNF is presented to illustrate its utility in guiding not only model development but also graph data augmentation, as well as graph engineering strategies aimed at enhancing trained models' fairness and accuracy.

This research focuses on kinetic models for reversible enzyme reactions and evaluates the effectiveness of two analytical techniques in obtaining approximate solutions to these models. We apply and compare the Homotopy Perturbation Method and the Simple Iteration Method to derive approximate analytical solutions to non-linear equations describing reversible enzyme reactions.  The resulting approximations demonstrate a comparable level of accuracy.  Supporting Matlab codes for both methods are provided in the appendices.

Theoretical models predict that natural and split supersymmetry could resolve the Higgs boson's mass by addressing its potential for stability. This research focuses on the most likely outcome of proton-proton collisions, which occur when the decay of a light top squark or gluino results in final states characterized by one or more jets and significant transverse momentum. The analysis relies on data from the CMS experiment at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV, spanning a considerable range of masses, including those that compete with the Higgs' stability threshold. The results were derived from events featuring exactly one or two leptons, a considerable number of jets, and substantial transverse momentum. The data analyzed accounted for 35.9 fb$^{-1}$ of integrated luminosity, yielding exclusions that surpassed the expected sensitivity by a considerable margin. This research excluded top squark and gluino possibilities, with the excluded masses consistent with models predicting the Higgs' stability's limits.

Two proposed expectation models for temporary financial bubbles, involving individuals with varied predictions and positive influences, show that bubble collapse can be marked by an explosive growth in prices that suddenly ends at a potential critical point. The varied predictions among rational individuals make it difficult to synchronize their actions, causing the bubble to survive nearly up to its expected endpoint. Exact solutions from the models yield mathematical transformations enabling new tests for detecting bubbles in financial trends, thus providing tools for identifying bubble onset and forecasting termination points. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through numerical examples illustrating bubble identification and forecasting using the S&P 500 index.

Quantum harmonic oscillators were computationally analyzed in their ground state with either steady-state driving forces varying in intensity or driving forces that changed over time. Calculations of position expectations were carried out for multiple scenarios of mass, angular frequency, and the lambda parameter in both cases. Constant driving led to coherent states, with theoretical predictions closely matched by both simulation approaches. Variations of this basic scenario led to mixed states, with the Markov Chain Monte Carlo method successfully utilized to account for these. Constant driving led to coherent states, with theoretical predictions closely matched by both simulation approaches. Variations of this basic scenario led to mixed states, with the Markov Chain Monte Carlo method successfully utilized to account for these. Constant driving led to coherent states, with theoretical predictions closely matched by both simulation approaches.

Recent research has shown significant progress in improving recommender system performance through leveraging reviews for predicting ratings, however the current methods have several limitations. The existing techniques often use complex neural networks, which make it challenging to easily understand reviewer sentiments. Moreover, they tend to overlook the unique interaction between reviews and users/items, resulting in poor generalization to unseen reviews and items. To overcome these challenges, a new approach called Sentiment-aware Interactive Fusion Network (SIFN) has been proposed, which accurately captures reviewer sentiment and enables seamless sharing of features between reviews, users, and items. The SIFN model consists of a review encoding module that encodes reviews via CNN, a interactive fusion module that computes interactive features through a multi-modal attention mechanism, and a prediction module that estimates rating predictions using review-aware review/item user features. The SIFN model outperforms state-of-the-art methods on several real-world datasets and showcases the effectiveness of review sentiment and interactive features.

Developing CS NLP systems is obstructed by a severe data scarcity. To address this issue, researchers use data augmentation techniques by incorporating CS text from various sources. However, existing studies primarily rely on English-Arabic CS data, neglecting a significant portion of Arabic-English CS data. This paper aims to close this research gap by developing various lexical replacement methods to effectively generate high-quality Arabic-English CS text. We introduce two English-Arabic CS corpora and compare the efficiency of 12 data augmentation approaches, including one novel lexical replacement method, to enhance CS modeling. The results reveal that using lexical replacement on non-consecutive source words can significantly boost CS modeling performance, ultimately ranking first among all examined techniques.

We show that any subgroup of homeomorphisms of a compact surface that fix the boundary, whose action within the surface's interior is highly transitive, cannot be topologically compact when using the compact-open topology's inherited structure.

We investigate integrable boundary conditions that can coexist with the generalized lambda deformations of Abelian and non-Abelian gauge theories. The bulk of the discussion centers on the Abelian case; preliminary analyses are, however, conducted for non-Abelian scenarios well-suited for simple evaluations. The Brane-Gauge/Boundary=Geometry method is utilized to determine the effective gauge field profiles in the probe brane's vicinity. Consequently, this method is applied to derive the entanglement entropy of specific probe branes as a function of the lambda parameter within the four-dimensional Maxwell gauge theory.

As tasks increasingly rely on computer vision, the importance of image processing has also grown, with applications like object recognition, autonomous driving, and medical visualization. While researchers have explored efficient methods for computing Laplacian and centroidal Voroni diagrams using hexagonal tiles, they often impose strict constraints such as a minimum object size. Our goal is to develop a flexible algorithm that can handle any object size, using a variable number of tetrahedra per hexagon, resulting in up to 58 percent fewer constraints than existing methods. To achieve this, we introduce a novel and efficient variant of the Lloyd's algorithm that utilizes tetrahedral constraints to distribute points within each hexagonal cell, allowing us to control the approximate number of tetrahedra per hexagon from 1 to 58. To ensure the integrity of the resulting hexagonal mesh, we also propose an algorithm that identifies and removes non-ideal hexagons through edge reconfigurations, demonstrating that our method outperforms existing approaches by using fewer tetrahedra while maintaining a similar accuracy.

The tasks of relation extraction and knowledge graph link prediction share a
common link in their objectives, allowing them to complement each other in the
process of predicting a subject-object relationship in a sentence. Specifically,
when a model identifies an object and its related subject, this relationship can
be utilized by another model to anticipate a list of potential objects associated
with the subject, indicating the original object should also be included in the
list. In our study, we utilized this connection by implementing a multi-stage
approach, training an initial relation extraction model followed by a knowledge
graph link prediction model that incorporates the results from the initial model.
Our results reveal that this combination results in higher accuracy and more
robust results compared to utilizing existing models in relation extraction.

This study introduces an innovative analytical delay model specifically tailored for deep submicron CMOS inverters. Developed based on the critical recognition that inverter delay is a complex interplay of multiple process variables, the proposed model incorporates just three independent parameters that define the device's transfer characteristic. Achieved through meticulous extraction of an accurate transistor current model, the analytical delay model exhibits remarkable precision in delaying prediction by less than 5% compared to SPICE simulations for a wide range of technological parameters. Furthermore, the flexibility of Matlab's Curve Fitting Toolbox facilitates effortless incorporation into an SPICE-compatible simulation environment, enriching design automation with rapid and reliable design optimization.

Making optimal decisions in complex, continuously changing environments requires
assuming certain conditions. Often, researchers assume a certain level of consistency
in the decision-making model known as the Q-function. However, in numerous real-world scenarios,
this condition does not hold true. Instead, we propose a more adaptable way of measuring the consistency of Q-functions
in various complex environments. This new approach enables us to establish tighter limits on our model's behavior, resulting
in improved learning efficiency. Additionally, we provide a theoretical understanding of how our measure of consistency
affects learning in these unique scenarios and offer practical applications to reward shaping.

The underlying mechanisms of the ventral temporal cortex's animacy organization remain contentious, suggesting that animacy exists along a spectrum rather than a binary divide. Recent evidence suggests this continuum is rooted in distinct processes: one involving facial expertise and the other based on movement perception. The animacy spectrum may be defined by the integration of these processes, which are in turn influenced by distinct factors such as object categorization and handedness. The following study investigates this, presenting data suggesting that movement information contributes to the spectrum more prominently in the anterior than in the posterior parts of the ventral temporal cortex. Furthermore, it appears that facial expertise is particularly prominent in the intermediate areas. When considering handedness, it is the left posterior brain area responsible for hand preference that makes a significant contribution to the animacy spectrum. The findings support the proposal of a unified animacy organization, supported by the unique role of movement information, facial expertise, and the complex interaction of categorical knowledge.

In scientific simulation, achieving accurate replication of real-world scenarios is a top priority. However, commonly used numerical methods, such as the finite element and finite volume methods, often introduce artifacts like negative density values, especially in the simulation of nonlinear physical phenomena like elastic plasticity and fluid dynamics. These negative values can lead to inaccurate results like the appearance of fine features in case of fluid dynamics. To address this, filtered methods are used to preserve essential data, like density, without affecting the location of key points like singularities. Our paper presents a new filtered formulation that ensures positive density and other crucial properties, without impacting the location of key data structures. This approach is based on a novel optimization framework that utilizes a suitable metric for measuring the distance between original and filtered data. Our proposal is compared against traditional renormalization techniques, showing that it has significant advantages in terms of accuracy and its ability to preserve key data properties, without adding additional layers of complexity. Our filtered formulation is also applied to complex 2D and 3D fluid dynamics simulations, demonstrating its ability to preserve key data properties like density and ensure the positivity of velocity values.

Quasi-periodic oscillations type C, typically observed in low-hard and hard-intermediate states of black hole X-ray transients, have been investigated using the MAXI J1535-571 data collected by Insight-HXMT. By applying a novel time-dependent Comptonization model and a relativistic reflection model, researchers have demonstrated its ability to accurately describe X-ray data up to 100 keV in the hard-intermediate state. Observations show that this model allows for the evolution of the electron phoat in density, consistent with expected patterns in the hard-intermediate state. However, the model fails to accurately explain spectra above 100 keV, which can be resolved by incorporating a corona component using a different Comptonization model. Building on this discovery, researchers have analyzed data from the type C QPO state and found that a realistc model similar to the one used in the hard-intermediate state can accurately describe X-ray data up to 100 keV. Nonetheless, the model fails to account for the spectral feature above 100 keV in this state, which can be resolved by incorporating a hot and dense region within the corona. Notably, the average spectral feature around 15-20 keV observed in this state cannot be explained by either model and may require the presence of a separate component.

In the context of multi-agent reinforcement learning, particularly for tasks requiring cooperation and communication, MARL agents are prone to deviating from their learned policies when they are used in scenarios with different partner agents. This problem arises from the lack of internal guidance that guides them to learn policies that are flexible enough to adapt to various partner behaviors. To address this issue, a new method called transfer empowerment is proposed, which integrates intrinsic motivation with imitation learning to enable efficient MARL in diverse partner behaviors. By leveraging empowerment as an intrinsic motivation, this method focuses on exploring the policy space that is most relevant to the given partner behavior, thus achieving better sample efficiency and more robustness in scenarios with different partner agents. The experimental results confirm the proposed method's ability to efficiently learn flexible policies that are immune to changes in partner behaviors.

We're introducing MatSim, a comprehensive synthetic dataset of textured 3D models, carefully crafted to accurately depict a wide variety of real-world materials texturing behaviors. MatSim encompasses 3D models with diverse materials, each displayed from multiple viewpoints with either glossy or matte finishes, and also includes partially occluded images. This balanced and extensive dataset caters to various material classes, simulating real-world scenarios where materials can be partially exposed or covered. The dataset is designed to facilitate the development of models capable of generalizing material attributes to unfamiliar contexts. To leverage MatSim for training, we incorporated a novel physics-based rendering system that utilizes the Bidirectional Surface Area Integration algorithm to accurately simulate real-world material appearances. To further enhance MatSim, we incorporated a dataset of real material images to fine-tune our 3D models and ensure they conform to known real-world material standards. We demonstrated MatSim's effectiveness through comparative experiments with existing state-of-the-art methods, showcasing its ability to efficiently process material recognition tasks across both novel and existing classes.

Two equivalent formulations of Lie 2-algebras are recalled: one as a categorification of Lie algebras and another as 2-term L∞-algebras. The paper proceeds by introducing four different types of Lie 2-algebras derived from 2-plectic manifolds, Courant algebroids, homotopy Poisson manifolds and multivector fields on a Lie groupoid. The Lie 2-algebra cohomology is also reintroduced and its lower-degree instances analyzed. The integration of strict Lie 2-algebras to strict Lie 2-groups is also a point of discussion in the paper.

We introduce a novel method for local image feature matching, where instead of a sequential process, we first identify pixel-wise dense matches at a basic level and then refine the good matches to extract detailed features. Unlike dense matching, we don't confine ourselves to pixels and use a self-attention mechanism to focus on relevant information. This approach has the added benefit of allowing us to simultaneously estimate transformation parameters and detailed features in a refined state. Experimental results showcase LoFTR's capability to accurately localize on challenging image datasets (7 Scenes, TUM, and CMU Visual Ambulatory Clinic Dataset) with high geometric accuracy and outperformstate-of-art methods, all while using fewer computational resources.

The paper addresses the problem of bias in vector magnetic field maps, particularly in estimating component values and their uncertainties. It attributes this bias to inaccuracies in the forward modeling of measurement noise levels. The study evaluates the impact of three bias correction methods on the vector magnetic field data, involving the use of (1) constant multipliers, (2) field-by-field iterative corrections, and (3) dembias coefficients derived from magnetic field templates. Among these, the third approach yields the most favorable results, as it provides optimal cancellation of bias and enables the reliable application of forward modeling to magnetograms. The successful dembiasing of magnetograms leads to improved vector magnetic field data and enhanced forward modeling performance, allowing for accurate derivation of atmospheric parameters such as $\beta\) and $S_{8/3}.$

This research paper explores a real-world scenario in which consumers selfishly aim to minimize their energy bills by scheduling their energy usage in advance. To effectively persuade these consumers to use less energy during peak hours and fairly compensate them for their remaining energy consumption, this study develops an automated demand response system. It frames the interaction between consumers and a retailer as an aggregative game with transferable payoffs, allowing for the determination of the unique Nash equilibrium through the linear complementarity problem. Additionally, to address consumers' noncooperative and unpredictable nature, the retailer implements time-varying pricing that adjusts based on current peak demand, while also designing a novel instant load billing mechanism to influence consumers' decisions. Notably, the quantity of consumables like electricity, which have capacity limitations, require specific storage capabilities when partaken, leading to a distinct pricing model and peak reduction characteristics as compared to traditional commodities.

A more recent version of the Einstein theory, the Rastall theory, introduces a revised form of the conservation law by incorporating a divergence of the energy current, utilising the Einstein tensor. This model has the General Relativity theory as a specific instance. The present study investigates black string hole space-time with a non-zero charge within the framework of the Rastall theory, calculating Hawking temperatures for both chargeless and charged black strings. The analysis indicates that gravitational charges have a positive impact on the Hawking temperatures in the Rastall theory. Furthermore, the study examines the gravitational influence on the thermodynamic equilibrium of black strings.

Building on von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem, considering a commutative system of unitary transformations, we examine the properties of a measure that characterizes the spectral properties of almost periodic functions. Assuming certain weak bounds on the system's jump probabilities, we derive precise asymptotic rates of convergence for the time-averaged values of observables in the context of von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem.

The research on extremely old and metal-poor stars within our Galaxy is instrumental in grasping its chemical evolution and the origin of star formation. These stars are rare, and only five have been detected so far with a metal content below -5.0. Recent data released by the Gaia mission now offers the means to discover more such stars through its spectral sensors known as BP/RP, which are capable of detecting extremely metal-poor and old stars with temperatures ranging from 5000K to 6000K. This study presents an effective approach to identifying extremely metal-poly stars using the Gaia BP/RP sensors' spectra. First, a prepared database containing simulated spectra with varying levels of metallicity and helium content, as well as stellar temperature and surface gravity, is used for comparison purposes. Then, a technique that makes use of machine learning is employed to analyze the Gaia BP/RP spectra and determine the most suitable option from the prepared database, with the option including the application of a mild convolution effect to account for potential changes in spectral resolution. Following this, a quick assessment is conducted to identify any potential extremely metal-poor stars detected by the Gaia Gaia DR3, resulting in the identification of nine such stars, with the metal content of five of them estimated to be lower than -5.0. This new method is valuable in facilitating further research on the stars identified, including the application of precise methods such as fiber spectroscopy or high-resolution spectroscopy.

This research offers a comprehensive analysis of fire season severity through a unique perspective. By recognizing that high latitude regions experience fire seasons in both summer and winter, we can visualize the frequency of fires as they relate to geographical longitude and time. Utilizing Google Earth Engine to analyze 20 years of global burned area data, our findings reveal how these seasons change with each hemisphere. However, we also show that additional information is required to accurately predict fire activity in both summers and winters. Consequently, we created an analytical tool that combines long-term and short-term data, including geographical layout, temporal patterns, and satellite imagery of vegetation health, to forecast fire frequency. Results indicate that our model is highly precise, requiring minimal data updates, as it can be trained using Google Earth Net. Through testing, we've demonstrated the efficiency of our model, as it's able to forecast fires eight months in advance with an impressive 75% accuracy, as measured by the Magi index. Finally, we've observed the interconnection of fire seasons across continents and revealed how local fires can affect distant regions, as seen with the 2019 Australian fires.

We've conducted a thorough examination of eight distinct methods for evaluating the morphological intricacy of languages. These measures have different prerequisites for data annotation, yet our study identifies both similarities and disparities among them. We compare the methods visually and statistically to ascertain how they correlate with typological characteristics. This investigation seeks to determine whether these metrics assess the same underlying aspect of language or, alternatively, measure different facets of morphological complexity. The results from principal component analysis suggest that a significant portion of variation across the eight measures is linearly associated.

Researchers at Meneghetti et al have discovered an increased occurrence of small gravitational lens effects within nearby galaxy clusters.  To examine the impact of self-interacting dark matter on these lens effects, three models based on Gurrado's equation were developed and tested.  These models, which vary according to their mass loss types, were applied to stronger lens maps within the COSMOS field to calculate mass-intrinsic alignment properties.  While the models indicate a weak correlation between mass and intrinsic alignment, this effect appears to be reduced by non-zero self-interaction in mass-intrinsic alignment properties, which is consistent with no significant difference in lens strength between NFW and \$\alpha-\beta\$ models.

This research focuses on reducing the complexity of parametric partial differential equations (PPDEs) by finding an accurate approximation space for the solutions of the equations. Given incomplete information, we use two primary sources: initial assumptions about the solutions and partial measurements from the equations. Based on these sources, we have developed methods to generate effective approximation subspaces and analyzed their performance. By identifying the optimal performance limit and providing simplified methods to achieve it, we have made strides in addressing the challenges associated with reducing the dimensionality of PPDE solutions while accounting for incomplete information about the equations and their solutions.

This research introduces the m-arcsinh Kernel ('m-ar-K') Fast Independent Component Analysis ('FastICA') approach ('m-ar-K-FastICA') for feature extraction, combining kernel-based dimensionality reduction with ICA to overcome the limitations of previous methods. Although the kernel trick offers a powerful way to tackle non-linearity, its effectiveness can be undermined by a lack of open-source and reproducible kernel selection protocols, which has slowed the adoption of this approach in neuroscience. The proposed m-ar-K-FastICA approach uses a novel arc-sinh kernel, whose parameters are optimized using an open-source, reproducible method. The suggested method is evaluated using publicly available EEG data from the BCI Competition IV. We provide the source code on GitHub at https://github.com/HesamRazavizadeh/m-ar-K-FastICA.

Identifying trending social media events in real-time across various geographical locations is crucial, particularly for anticipating incidents such as accidents, protests, or breaking news. The dynamic nature of social media data poses challenges to traditional approaches, including ambiguous event timelines and spaces. An innovative solution, this research introduces an adaptive spatio-temporal event detection framework leveraging social media. It addresses spatial resolution ambiguity through a quad-tree based method that segmentates regions based on data density, and uses statistical analysis incorporating the Poisson distribution to highlight anomalies in post density. Furthermore, event duration is determined by filtering simultaneous events and tracking their evolution, and filtering is applied to eliminate irrelevant data. An implementation of this framework, called SEDE, is realized using Apache Flink, a distributed processing engine, incorporating the Elasticsearch query language for data analysis. An evaluation of SEDE is conducted using two datasets, and its performance is compared with existing approaches, demonstrating its effectiveness in detecting precise spatial and temporal events. The results show that SEDE efficiently handles social media data with competitive performance, and its capabilities in processing real-time data are verified through an experimental analysis of various query patterns. An evaluation of SEDE highlighting its capabilities in detecting real-time events, such as the 2017 Barcelona Attack, is also provided.

We establish the optimal Lipschitz regularity of very weak solutions for the measure-valued elliptic PDE $-\mathrm{div}(A(x) \nabla u) = Q \; \mathcal{H}^{n-1} \llcorner \Gamma$ within a smooth domain $\Omega$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$. Here, $\Gamma$ represents a $C^{1,\alpha}$-smooth hypersurface, with $Q$ defined as a $C^{0,\alpha}$ density on $\Gamma$, and $A$ characterizes a symmetric, uniformly elliptic and $W^{1,q}$-regular tensor $(q > n)$. Furthermore, the article examines the optimality of these conditions applied to the problem data. This particular equation essentially represents a special interface coupling of two $A$-harmonic functions, with implications for free boundary problems, to be discussed in detail.

Advanced permanent magnets made from rare earth and transition metal alloys achieve high magnetization by containing a high amount of the transition metal, as seen in YCo$_{15}$, whereas less expensive, low-cost alternatives made from rare earth and boron only contain transition metal in small amounts, resulting in lower magnetization, but are still widely used. By combining the strengths of high-throughput calculations and an optimization technique called evolutionary search, researchers discovered several promising magnetic materials within the binary system of yttrium, cobalt, and boron. Notably, they found that by varying the ratio of Y to Co, the number of cobalt atoms can be increased while maintaining the stability of the hexagonal Fe$_{2}$Mn$_{5}$ (Hoffman phase) and Mn$_{5}$Fe$_{1-x}$Co$_{x}$ (Skutterudite phase) structures. This phase stability, as well as the enhanced magnetization resulting from increased cobalt, was also observed in the hexagonal Fe$_{2}$Mn$_{5}$ and Skutterudite phases of another metal system, Fe$_{5}$Co$_{11}$, by adding a small amount of Ni to the compound Fe$_{5}$Co$_{6}$, resulting in the increased cobalt content of Fe$_{5}$Co$_{11}$.

In the field of display advertising, real-time bidding has become the predominant approach. Each ad impression resulting from user page loading is instantly auctioned off, with demand-side platforms (DSPs) providing bids typically based on the value of the resulting ad impression and optimal bid price. However, this common practice of providing a single optimal bid price proves insufficient when accounting for the unpredictability of ad impression values and the constraints on a DSP's daily expenditure. To address these limitations, this study introduces an adaptive bidding strategy that dynamically adjusts the bid price in response to the bid request's unique characteristics, including available budget and the uncertainty of resulting estimates. By doing so, this bidding strategy is capable of meeting a DSP's expenditure goal while minimizing the overall cost of a DSP's daily expenditure. To evaluate the effectiveness of this adaptive bidding strategy, a series of numerical simulations were conducted.

Nonclassical properties in continuous-variable quantum systems are often marked by quantum correlations and Wigner negativity. This study explores how these two nonclassical traits are connected in the context of remotely generating Wigner negativity in one subsystem given another's specific measurement. Research has previously established that when Alice and Bob share a Gaussian state, Bob can create Wigner negativity in Alice's system through measurement, if and only if there is a steering influence from Alice's to Bob's system. This study expands on these findings to consider a more diverse set of scenarios, including non-Gaussian states shared by Alice and Bob. The research demonstrates that when Alice's measurements on Bob's system yield positive Wigner functions, Bob can create Wigner negativity in Alice's subsystem, and this is directly linked to the degree of quantum steering from Bob's to Alice's system. Notably, the study finds that weaker steering corresponds to less Wigner negativity created by Bob's measurements, and this relationship remains even if Bob's measurements yield negative Wigner functions.

Accurate secure boundary analysis is crucial for practical quantum key distribution systems, but the current approach overlooks a critical aspect – the randomness consistency of seeds used in privacy amplification. We introduce and prove a quantum leftover hash lemma that applies to non-uniform random seeds, leveraging min-entropy, and subsequently establish a detailed, precise QKD secure boundary analysis. Utilizing the two-decoy BB84 protocol, we simulate the application of our hash lemma in a specific scenario and calculate the secure boundary under real-world conditions, considering effects like vacuum, single-photon, and multi-photon pulses, as well as systematic errors in measurement results.

This research paper confirms that certain types of curves, specifically those in higher dimensional space, do not fit the classification of Bertrand curves except in two-dimensional Euclidean space. A new category, called the timelike (1,3)-Bertrand curve, is defined to fill this gap and its characteristics are identified for curves in a four-dimensional Euclidean space.

In this work, we explore diagrammatic methods in waveguide QED systems with a particular focus on systems utilizing delayed coherent quantum feedback. By using a specific mathematical approach within the rotating wave approximation, we demonstrate that N-particle scattering matrices in single-mode channels can be expressed as a combination of (N-1) particle scattering matrices, under certain conditions regarding particle interactions. This mathematical relationship is the foundation for a detailed physical interpretation and is further exemplified through its application in two types of systems: the Tavis-Cummings model and the Dicke model.

A potential way to study low-mass dark matter is by utilizing boosted dark matter interactions. The framework for light dark matter interactions involving no spin is relatively well-established, but the same cannot be said for spin-dependent interactions. The current analysis provides the first comprehensive examination of the scattering cross-section for boosted dark matter with spin dependence. By building on existing work regarding Earth-based dark matter detection experiments, this study develops a formula to calculate the total scattering cross-section. It initially considers the case where dark matter and nuclear target share no spins, followed by an extension to account for spins in the latter. The resulting expression includes terms related to boosted dark matter velocity and its angular distribution. The study also assesses velocity and angle factors that contribute to scattered dark matter and determines the most significant terms for subGeV dark matter, assuming no spin. The analysis further extends to binary black hole mergers with an emphasis on evaluating post-scattering terms relevant to gravitational wave events. The study also examines in detail post-scattering terms relevant to gravitational wave events, with a focus on binary black hole mergers. By building on existing work regarding LIGO's detection experiments, this analysis develops formulas to calculate the probability that a particular detector will detect such events. The study however concludes that by comparing calculated and modified post-scattering terms, this analysis reveals notable distinctions between low and high velocity post-scattering terms, with a sharp increase, as does the post-scattering term in certain direction, with a certain threshold velocity.
