Graphene with gaps has been proposed to showcase the valley Hall effect, where different types of electron flows, determined by specific indices, are observed.  However, the phenomenon was challenged upon realizing that the indices can be redefined, leading to an alternative effect described as the orbital Hall effect, where a single type of electron flow is maintained, but varying magnetic Chern numbers across different orbital indices result in distinct orbital Hall conductivities.  The viability of the orbital Hall effect is demonstrated through a quasi-periodic model representing a moiré superlattice, where the orbital Hall effect is revealed, but intriguingly, its combination with the orbital Hall effect leads to an alternating pattern of orbital Hall conductivity.

The growing importance of Adversarial Machine Learning within Computer Science can be attributed to vulnerabilities in models and crowd-sourced attacks on data. Over the past two years, research has gained momentum in graph adversarial attacks but Graph Classification remains an understudied area. The indirect utilization of Reinforcement Learning methods for graph classification, given that datasets involve discrete graphs with labels, stands in contrast to traditional approaches. Our work identifies limitations in existing graph classification models and introduces a novel reinforcement learning strategy to exploit Graph GAN vulnerabilities in graph classification. The exploitation involves generating and introducing noise into the training dataset to decrease the model's accuracy. Our method is tested successfully on the NCI-ABoS dataset, with results including constructed sets that lower the model's accuracy and evidence of transferred attacks across multiple models.

The process of matching objects between photometric catalogs can lead to problems when objects of different magnitudes are matched together. This issue can be resolved by only considering matches where the objects have similar flux ratios. The effect of a cross-match protocol, which incorporates both photometric and astrometric criteria, has been compared to one that focuses solely on astrometry. The results from mock catalogs show that incorporating astrometric information significantly boosts the success rate of the cross-match, especially for objects of lower magnitude. The greatest improvement is seen for objects at the brightest end with a magnitude difference threshold of 1.0, resulting in a near-perfect match, exceeding 90% success rate. The incorporation of photometric information, however, also yields substantial gains, although to a lesser extent. Ultimately, the optimal cross-match protocol relies on the specific characteristics of the catalogs in question and may benefit from being tailored according to magnitude.

In this paper, a hypergraph is considered as the family of its edges, and a hypergraph is said to possess a k-minimal dominating family if for every edge, there exists at least one member of the family such that removing it still results in a family that dominates all the edges of the original family. Additionally, a hypergraph is said to possess a k-minimal minimal dominating family if for every edge, there exists at most k-minimal families dominating all the edges of the original family. Furthermore, a hypergraph is said to possess a k-minimal covering family such that for every edge, there exists at most k families covering all the edges of the original family. We present the Inf-HY(k) and HY(k)-min family as the families of k-minimal dominating and k-minimal minimal dominating families, respectively, in infinite hypergraphs, and the HY(c)-cof family as the family of the edges not contained in any k-minimal covering family, respectively. We show the equivalence of the families under a certain condition and provide an example of a hypergraph with the family of its edges being a HY(k)-cof and HY(k+1)-cof at the same time. We investigate the relationship between the densities of the Inf-HY(k) and HY(k) for a hypergraph and show that it is directly proportional to the k. We generalize the concept of the Turan hypergraph problem and investigate the upper limit of the size of the Inf

Domain-specific knowledge is frequently captured using comprehensive, formally structured concept relationships called ontologies. In fields like biology and medicine, vast ontologies comprise hundreds of thousands of interconnected concepts. Effective visual representations are particularly crucial when dealing with large, complex ontologies, enabling easier comprehension and navigation. Although existing visualisation tools primarily focus on hierarchical structures and overlooked the analysis of interconnected associations, we developed a new method and tool, OntoPlot, to showcase non-hierarchical relationships within comprehensive ontologies. By incorporating innovative visual components, we successfully enhanced the understanding and identification of associated associations. We present OntoPlot, a novel visualisation tool that facilitates the exploration and analysis of shared connections within large ontologies, resulting in an accessible and user-friendly tool that aids in understanding and navigating complex domain-specific knowledge.

We introduce an innovative technique that synergistically combines inter-domain loss and CycleGAN to facilitate semi-supervised end-to-end automatic speech recognition. Inter-domain loss aims to derive a common speech-nicegph feature representation, whereas CycleGAN, as a type of unsupervised domain adaptation method, maps auxiliary data with a domain discrepancy to the speech domain. Our experimental findings on the WSJ, Voxforge, and LibriSpeech datasets reveal significant improvements, with relative decreases in error rates observed as high as 25%.

A fundamental theory known as active inference underpins how living beings interact with their surroundings. This theory views the brain as an efficient tool that employs Bayesian principles to create a detailed mental framework, aiming to minimize uncertainty about the world. Despite the theory's significance in cognitive neuroscience, its practical application is restricted to simplified simulations due to limitations in dealing with large and varied environments. The challenge lies in the computational expense of processing high-resolution sensor data, such as vision, and navigating through complex spaces efficiently. To overcome this, we introduce a novel approach that combines the principles of active inference, object detection using faster R-CNN, and deep reinforcement learning with predictive models. This approach associates sensor data with a condensed representation of the mental framework, reducing processing requirements. The results show that this approach can successfully allow simulated robots to independently navigate and achieve desired goals in more complex environments. Furthermore, we discuss how this method can inform future research in cognitive neuroscience, specifically with regard to brain-inspired mental frameworks that are not limited by the constraints of the existing simulation software.

Our study of binary mixtures used molecular dynamics simulations out of equilibrium to explore the Soret effect, particularly the influence of flexible molecules' internal freedom on this phenomenon. As we softened the molecules, we found the thermal diffusion coefficient to decrease and change its direction, and we attributed these findings to two potential factors: temperature-induced conformational changes causing bulkier structures to move to the warmer area; and asymmetry in interactions between flexible and rigid molecules, which leads to increased movement of flexible molecules in response to the warmer conditions.

The development of Automated Essay Scoring involves a fusion of expertise from Education, Linguistics, and Natural Language Processing. Effective evaluation by an NLP model depends on its ability to identify patterns in written content, even in cases where the writing quality is subpar. Despite the current prominence of BERT and RoBERTa models in ASE, a significant limitation is their slow training pace and resource-intensive nature. A better approach is to utilize efficient models such as RoBERTa and BERT, with variants like DeBERTa and BART, to accurately score and analyze essay content. Given the prominent role of ELMo models in the ASE field, another suitable model to train on this task is the ELMo-based model, or a more enhanced version, ELROBERTa, which we find to be better than the original model. A comprehensive evaluation of these efficient models reveals that DeBERTa and ELROBERTa stand out as superior alternatives to standard models like BERT and RoBERTa, with the added advantage of being more suitable for educational ASE tasks due to their reduced parameter count, making them ideal substitutes for standard models, specifically in the case of ELMo-based models.

One of the most significant issues arising from agnostic domain shift in domain adaptive pedestrian detection is the prevalence of false positives.  As labeling each target domain's boxes is a labor-intensive task, most approaches suppress false positives based on top-ranked boxes, leading to incomplete removal of faults.  In this research, a new strategy, the Re-Ranking method, is proposed to further refine the suppression results.  First, a pseudo-label loss function is used to update the bounding boxes, leading to improved confidence scores.  Next, a box loss function is used to update the box embeddings, allowing for enhanced similarity between positive boxes.  Finally, a background/foreground balance loss function is used to balance the two classes, allowing for the adaptation of feature representations.  Our experiments show significant improvements, with up to 84.3% reduction in false positives compared to state-of-the-art approaches.

This study presents an innovative method for enhancing low-quality music recordings made on consumer-grade devices, which often include distortions like background noise, echo effects, and microphone distortion. A novel deep learning technique combines two processes: one transforms audio in a specific representation called the mel-spectrogram into a new, more desirable format, and another converts synthetically created mel-spectrograms into high-quality audio waves that are perceptually natural-sounding. Experimental results indicate that this approach surpasses established methods, which apply more conventional techniques for reversing the mel-spectrogram process and another technique directly translating noisy audio waves to clear ones. Moreover, the research also examines the dependability of typical audio improvement evaluation metrics in the context of music by conducting a listening test.

Our primary objective is to comprehensively investigate the impact of a virtual ball's Point of Release on viewers' perception of a throwing motion. Our perceptual study revealed that individuals tend to more readily notice errors in underarm throws where the point of release occurs early, in contrast to late releases. Conversely, in the case of overarm throws, participants generally have a harder time identifying errors with an early point of release, as opposed to a late release. Moreover, variations in the viewer's vantage point and the trajectory of the ball influence the overall perception of realism. These research findings can potentially contribute to the improvement of the realism presented in tasks such as virtual try-out operations or sports video games.

To efficiently decode the hierarchy of translations, an existing approach known as Syntax-Guided Neural Machine Translation uses Syntax-based Dependency Parsing to limit the possible translations. However, this method always starts from the topmost dependency relationship and makes decisions about each parent independently, which results in suboptimal translations and slow decoding speeds. In order to overcome these limitations, we developed a new decoding algorithm called Top-Down Syntax-Guided Decoding, which iteratively adds dependency relationships in a bottom-up order and ensures that all possible translations for each relationship are considered. This algorithm is combined with a unique tree structured decoding model called Top-DTSD, which includes explicit connections between nodes that reflect the tree's structure. This model can also be used in an analysis-by-incidence-scoring manner, and experiments have shown that it surpasses previous methods in both translation and parsing performance.

The credibility of astrochemical simulations largely relies on the accuracy of binding energy values that take into account the diverse structures and energy patterns found at ice-grain surface areas. Existing astrochemical models primarily rely on the average binding energies, despite the complex distributions of energies observed. The new Binding Energy Evaluation Platform aims to provide access to the complete spectrum of binding energies derived through first-principles calculations, complementing the current best practices in the field. Being an open-source web-based client-server system, the platform can easily accommodate updates and expansions to include further ice models, other interstellar solvents, and the calculation of other desorption energies. The platform's design also enables the generation of binding energy distributions based on experimental data. By showcasing its capabilities with two specific examples related to hydrogen-bonded water clusters on amorphous carbon dioxide, the platform demonstrates its ability to simulate binding energy distributions for hydrogen-bonded water molecules on CO2 ice grains relevant to the TMC-1 source. The platform is available online at http://www.binding-energy.net.

A multiplicative stochastic process with lognormally distributed lower bounds is studied, where a theoretical model of the process is developed and its distribution, characterized by four parameters, along with its statistical properties, is analytically determined. This model is further validated by demonstrating its compatibility with real-world data through parameter adjustment.

We offer novel approaches to acquire in-depth knowledge about a mysterious quantum state using an efficiently manageable number of copies. Our key contribution is a depth-controlled randomized measurement strategy involving a series of controlled rotation, which enables us to calculate key statistics regarding a general density matrix, without needing to have prior information about its form. Our method is specifically tailored for matrices that can be broken down into a combination of simple states, and it uses low-depth sequences of controlled rotation. Our investigation also encompasses the application of our technique to degenerate eigenstates and scenarios where the state of a quantum system can be described by a limited set of parameters. Our outcome includes an efficiently manageable number of copies-based method, which enables us to estimate key properties like the presence of singularities, trace, and maximum eigenvalue in each parameter set. Our general approach is then applied to specific scenarios, such as a situation where the state of a quantum system can be described by a limited set of parameters with constant coefficients. Our investigation also encompasses the application of our technique to specific models, such as the Hemeriting Franklin model and the Truncated Haagerman-Lee-Mueller (THLM) model.

The researchers in a particular field with equations known as Davey-Stewartson II explore how waves behave under reflection off a calm surface. They are particularly interested in how this interaction changes the frequency of the waves and the path the waves travel under specific conditions. In order to address this question, they study how the waves' behavior changes in areas far from the reflection point in a small yet measurable range. It's discovered that the range of these changes can be broken down into two main parts: the behavior of the waves under strong or weak frequency conditions and the behavior of the waves when the calculation is done correctly or incorrectly based on the conditions. By studying these different cases, researchers find that under strong frequency conditions, the range of the waves' behavior depends on an important yet complex formula, while under weak frequency conditions, the range of the waves' behavior depends on several simpler formulas. In all cases, researchers are able to derive a complete set of mathematical equations that describe how the waves' behavior changes over time.

The vast majority of NLP text transformations have inherent limitations in their ability to expand coverage of input data due to the need to preserve the original message's meaning. In order to overcome this constraint, we propose a concept of sibylvariant transformations, which can successfully expand upon existing methods by using multiple possible interpretations of a given text. To study sibylvariant transformations, we developed a novel method of combining two models that focuses on detecting the most and least likely interpretations of a given text. Through our experiments with text classification, we found that this technique leads to better performance when implemented using transfer learning on datasets containing a wide variety of emotions, as it is particularly resilient to data that contains adversarial attacks.

Researchers aim to create meta-learning algorithms that capitalize on previous experience to rapidly acquire new skills or adapt to new environments by utilizing representation learning techniques, which enable the transfer of knowledge across various tasks. As the interest in meta-learning grows, there is a pressing need to establish its theoretical foundations, especially in terms of learning adaptable representations. In this research, we tackle the problem of multi-task linear regression where multiple related tasks share a common, low-dimensional linear representation. Our study provides effective, sample-efficient methods to address the dual challenges of learning a shared feature set from related tasks and transferring this knowledge to unseen tasks. This work sheds light on the central issue of meta-learning. Furthermore, we present theoretical limits on the minimum sample size required to learn these linear features.

Utilizing multilingual learning in state-of-the-art machine translation models can aid in adapting to low-resource languages despite limited data, albeit resulting in oversized models that are impractical for deployment. To address this issue, we examined the efficiency of model pruning and knowledge distillation in creating lightweight MT models for low-resource languages. While pruning significantly reduced model complexity, it proved highly unstable and inconsistent, with negative effects on BLEU scores in our experiments. In contrast, learning a distilled model yielded consistent results across our tests. Considering the stability and reliability of each approach, we recommend distillation as a more effective method for developing lightweight MT models in low-resource languages.

The Turan number for an r-uniform graph F, denoted by ex(n, F), is defined as the maximum number of edges in an F-free r-uniform graph on n vertices. The Turan density of F, denoted by pi(F), is defined as the limit of the maximum number of edges over the total possible number of edges as the number of vertices approaches infinity. Erdos-Stone-Simonovits' theorem established that the set of possible Turan densities for 2-uniform graphs is infinite, and for 3-uniform graphs, irrational Turan densities can be achieved, particularly those that are roots of 3, yet for 2-uniform graphs, irrational densities are yet to be found. This paper investigates irrational Turan densities for 2-uniform graphs, particularly focusing on a single hypergraph formed by a 4-set with a shared element, and demonstrates that there exists a sequence of such densities that approaches exactly one irrational number, specifically the irrational square root of 3.

The efficiency of deep learning semantic segmentation algorithms in medical imaging can be impacted by limited data. In our study, we evaluated the effectiveness of different data augmentation techniques on the performance of a U-Net model for pneumonia segmentation in chest X-rays. By analyzing five separate experiments, we found that combining rotation and flipping data augmentation methods resulted in the lowest Roche Index value of 0.22, yielding an accuracy of 83.11% and Roche Accuracy of 83.09% respectively.

Existing image captioning models often fail to produce captions according to the desired style just by adjusting hyperparameters. This paper proposes a novel framework for image captioning that uses prompts to regulate the output. We investigate various prompting techniques within Transformer architectures, identifying two key types - sentence prompting and token prompting - and demonstrating their effectiveness in transforming the output of a pre-trained model. Experiments conducted on COCO, Flickr8k, and Flickr30k reveal the flexibility of our approach in generating captions in multiple styles, and our source code is available for public use.

As autonomous systems become increasingly prevalent, it is essential to establish a legal and regulatory framework for addressing harm caused by these systems to individuals. Previous attempts to define harm in philosophical literature have failed to address various real-world examples, leading some to consider abandoning the concept of harm. The existing definitions of harm, largely reliant on causality, surprisingly overlook the use of causal models and actual causality theories. This paper presents a new definition of qualitative harm grounded in causal models and an interpretation of qualitative causal models, utilizing intrinsic equivalence and equvalency relations. The proposed approach is demonstrated to address challenges in existing literature, including a limit case involving self-harm, and is further evaluated in comparative reasoning.

This study showcases MMLSpark, an innovative open-source library that bridges the gap between Cognitive Toolkit and Apache Spark by introducing Java bindings and new components. The integration with OpenCV and the development of automated PySpark wrapper generation tool expands on Spark's capabilities, enabling easier use. The MMLSpark library is demonstrated through various use cases, including a deep learning application that utilizes Spark's DataFrames and the ability to add custom Java functionality via SparkJob.

Speech-to-text translation involves converting spoken language into written language 
from one language spoken to another language written in a different script. 
Current approaches rely on large amounts of paired speech and text, speech and text 
paired with translations, or simply a lot of text translations. This work shows how 
we can translate without preparation: by listening to speech in one language and 
transcribing it into another language without any training. This innovative 
methodology revolves around the idea that speech is universally consistent, 
irrespective of the language used. We implement this through a simple strategy, 
where the meaning of the speech is encoded, and then generated into a target 
language based on the source text. We manage to achieve this by utilizing electra, 
a pre-trained model that can change the text, and using speech recognition models 
that can convert speech into text. We successfully tested this approach on two 
sets of languages.

This work introduces a novel extension of the traditional heat conduction theory, encompassing cases with fading memory and incorporating the standard heat equation under dynamic boundary conditions as a particular instance. We delve into the well-posedness of systems comprised of equations akin to those by Coleman and Gurtin, further subject to dynamic boundary conditions with memory. These systems contain nonlinear elements situated both internally and on the boundary, with their behavior either dictated by classical dissipation principles or governed by a nonlinear balance condition. Moreover, one of the system components is accompanied by an evolution equation. These equations are analyzed in their three-dimensional formulation. By exploiting the properties of evolution operators, the paper proves the existence and uniqueness of solutions in various functional settings.

Precise short-term forecasts of energy consumption are essential for managing low voltage electricity networks efficiently, particularly with regard to highly disaggregated load distributions among a small number of customers, where individual behaviors tend to dominate aggregate consumption profiles. Since peak demand often drives energy distribution challenges, developing accurate timing and level predictions of daily peak demand is crucial, as traditional forecasting methods frequently struggle to characterize these spikes adequately. This issue renders current probabilistic forecasting methods, which typically excel at predicting base-load consumption, less effective during peak demand periods. Our approach tackles this limitation by fusing predictions from disaggregated models and peak demand forecasts, combining both base-load and peak characteristics to provide a more comprehensive forecast. This method incorporates the use of neural networks, support vector regression, and Gaussian processes, in addition to the standard extrapolation of peak demands, allowing us to assess the potential gain in forecasting accuracy throughout the prediction horizon. Our results show that the combination of disaggregated and peak forecasts surpasses the performance of pure extrapolation, yet the incorporation of peak forecasts does not significantly enhance the forecast accuracy in our dataset, which mainly consists of base-load consumption.

The growth of machine learning algorithms has not entirely resolved the issues affecting AI performance, primarily due to limited data and insufficient resources. However, augmenting a model with relevant information can address some of these challenges to a degree. The difficulty in effectively integrating knowledge lies in the multiple forms of knowledge representation involved. This paper aims to provide an overview of various knowledge integration approaches and their effectiveness in machine learning applications.

Creating a reliable model for precise COVID-19 detection on chest CT scans poses significant difficulties despite considerable advancements. The issue often arises due to annotation biases affecting traditional supervised segmentation techniques, which rely on detailed boundary markings. To resolve these issues and minimize labeling expenses, we introduce an innovative framework that utilizes image-level labels, thereby facilitating unbiased lesion detection and reducing data annotation costs. This data-driven framework pairs a generative adversarial network with a specialized decoder to distinguish lesions from the original images. Our experiments using two COVID-19 datasets confirm the efficiency and superior performance of this new approach compared to existing methods.

Accurate vertebrae localization and identification are crucial in various medical applications related to spine disorder diagnosis and surgical planning. However, certain pathological variations (e.g., vertebral compression fractures, scoliosis, and vertebral fixation) and imaging conditions (e.g., limited visibility, metal artifacts, and restricted spine mobility) make this task quite challenging. To address these difficulties, this paper presents a sophisticated and precise vertebra localization and identification framework, which works effectively under both normal and challenging circumstances. First, the proposed framework enhances 3D spine visibility by removing non-relevant information, rotating the spine to a standard orientation, and systematically exploring all possible vertebral levels. Next, vertebral boundaries in x-ray images are estimated using contextual information and optimized in a unified manner across the x-ray dataset. Building on these boundary estimates, the vertebral centerlines are calculated and used to develop a spatial context for vertebra identification. To achieve precise vertebra positioning, the proposed framework employs a novel optimization technique that incorporates anatomical constraints, optimizing vertebra positions in the form of a quadratic function, with solutions derived through a dual-process approach. Comprehensive testing of the proposed framework, utilizing 210 with normal spine conditions and 210 with scoliosis-related abnormalities, has yielded impressive localization and identification accuracy, with top scores achieved in both subjective human assessments (95.0% and 96.0%, respectively) and objective automated methods (94.7% and 95.7%, respectively).

Our theory explores the behavior of electron collisions with a strong repulsive barrier in a confined space as described by the S-matrix method. We've identified a novel strategy for temporarily safeguarding delicate particles by manipulating the space's boundary conditions. This approach could lead to a significant breakthrough in the field of ultrastrong light-matter coupling, where it may be possible to prevent particles from being destroyed by vacuum fluctuations.

In the field of legged locomotion, spring-based actuators can boost energy efficiency and performance but complicate the control algorithms. This research takes a new approach by using model-based control methods for an elastic legged robot, focusing on reducing dependence on simulation environments and impact on hardware durability. We developed a compact model integrating mechanical and electromagnetic properties of series-series elastic actuators, allowing for direct computation of actuator dynamics. This generated an augmented system comprising non-linear battery-actuator-dynamics, which was exploited in a model-predictive control method to enhance quadruped locomotion. We implemented this method on an elastic robot called MiniCheetah and found it to be as efficient as elastic-kmpc, a more traditional control technique, while significantly reducing computational requirements by a factor of 5 and runtime of 50%.

We propose a new variational quantum algorithm, the Variational Separability Verifier (VSV), to identify the closest separable state of an arbitrary quantum state with the largest margin of difference in fidelity between the given state and its closest separable counterpart and a completely mixed state. By abelianizing the problem, our algorithm's performance is demonstrated through successful characterization of necessary and sufficient conditions for separability in terms of eigenvalues and optimal entanglement measures, yielding the highest known precision for small systems. Furthermore, the method is applied to generate approximate separable superpositions in multi-qubit systems.

A well-documented phenomenon, parallel electron currents play a significant role in various laboratory and space plasmas. Research has demonstrated that these currents can amplify certain kinetic instabilities, such as the mirror instability, and protect against other growth rates. A specific computer-simulation study has now investigated the dynamics of a left-hand tearing mode in a hot, collisionless ion slab. The investigation showed that electron currents resulting from excess energy lead to an increase in the tearing instability growth rate. A specific result indicated a roughly linear relationship between this growth rate and the electron temperature. Additionally, the study found that the resulting mode amplitude exhibits exponential growth, reaches equilibrium within a particular time frame, and is influenced by finite-beta effects.

A surge in demand for search by image has led researchers to investigate fashion instance-level image retrieval, which involves finding matching images. Building upon this, the concept of fashion attribute manipulation, which modifies a specific attribute while retaining others, has emerged. This enables the creation of multiple images from a single baseline, facilitating improved search functionality. However, existing fashion attribute manipulation methods, primarily designed for search by attribute, have limitations in this area. In an effort to address these issues, we propose an innovative method that manipulates attributes at the feature level rather than the attribute level. This method adjusts feature maps instead of attributes, thereby preserving the original attributes. It's worth noting that our approach is unique in its focus on image retrieval. It can, however, be applied to other fields such as manipulation. In our experiments, we evaluated the proposed method's effectiveness in search by image, which demonstrated favorable results. Additionally, through a 1-shot setting, we showed that the proposed method can lead to better retrieval results, even when as little as one example is provided.

The $\R$-optimal solution for the underdetermined equation $Ax=y$ where $A$ is a bounded linear operator mapping a Banach space to a Hilbert space, and $\R$ is a strongly convex function defined in that space, is proven to converge strongly to the least squares estimate for the solution when the functional is the square of the norm of $y-Ax$, or when an $\epsilon$-ball is considered for that space, under the condition that the singular values of $A$ start at a positive value. A sequence of parameters that converges to zero is used to achieve this result, coupled with an iterative process that updates the estimate for the solution based on the gradient of the functional with respect to the current estimate, and the gradient of the norm with respect to the parameter. This process is denoted as the dual gradient process, and is applied iteratively to the two variables, until convergence is achieved. This algorithm, denoted as the dual gradient process for regularized problems, is shown to be a non-monotone method, and its behavior is analyzed through simulations for one and two dimensional problems. The study is then generalized to problems that involve multiple functions, and the behavior of the algorithm, denoted as the dual gradient process for the composite $\R$-functional, is analyzed using the principle of alternating direction dual matching pursuit.

Constructing the matching cost is a critical step in estimating light field depth but has received limited attention in the era of deep learning. The prevailing method in the field of deep learning constructs matching cost through the sequential shifting of each sub-aperture image with predefined offsets, making the process complex, laborious, and inefficient. This inefficiency leads to several issues, such as the increased requirement for computational resources and the inability of the model to accurately learn from the constructed matching cost. Therefore, this paper presents an innovative approach to constructing the matching cost, specifically designed for light field depth estimation. This novel constructor utilizes a geometrically accurate and statistically constant 3DLUT to streamline the matching cost calculation process, reducing its complexity and making it more efficient. The proposed approach also enables the model to accurately learn from the constructed matching cost and achieves enhanced performance, resulting in the improved SRLFDE method. The SRLFDE method demonstrates superior performance on the SIDD-LF, LFSD, and ESTEEM-LF datasets, with significant gains of $+0.36$, $+0.23$, and $+0.19$ dB in terms of peak signal-to-noise ratio, respectively. Moreover, the SRLFDE method outperforms its competitors while utilizing a reduced amount of computational resources. The SRLFDE method is publicly available at https://github.com/chenxi141/SRLFDE.

This study uses the bilinear method to investigate the Fokas-Lenells equations, first reducing the system and then employing double Wronskian solutions to yield a range of solutions for the reduced equations, resulting in a comprehensive overview of solutions for both classical and complex Lenells equations. Several examples illustrate this method's efficiency in deriving solutions for the Fokas-Lenells equations, particularly those displaying novel features such as rational behavior, singularities, and hyperbolic collisions. Furthermore, the analysis provides new insights into this system's integrability, particularly in the context of the inverse scattering method, while confirming prior findings regarding periodic solutions and the Kaup-Konopelchenko spectral problem.

Alternative theories of gravity that go beyond the Riemannian framework have been proposed to explore quantum gravity and model systems with non-relativistic symmetry. However, developing these theories involves a complex task: deriving an action principle that accurately captures their behavior. This technical note utilizes the formulation of double field theory to create action frameworks for these alternative gravity theories. By doing so, it resolves the ambiguities associated with their corresponding motion equations. As a result, this note embeds three theories – Torsional Newton-Cartan gravity, Carrollian gravity, and String Newton-Cartan gravity – within double field theory and derives their respective action frameworks for comparison with previously established literature results.

To meet growing demands for next-generation home WiFi networks, it is essential to improve their performance capabilities. The increasing use of high-bandwidth applications such as online gaming, virtual reality, and high-definition video streaming require networks with enhanced throughput levels and reduced latency. One effective strategy for achieving these goals is to deploy multiple access points within a given area, but this also leads to another issue: the need to manage signal overlap between these devices to prevent network interference. This is where the problem arises, as current methods used to mitigate this challenge often fail to adapt to dynamic changes within the network, causing performance degradation under high-traffic conditions. To address this limitation, we propose a novel solution that leverages the capabilities of IEEE 802.11k/v standards to allow WiFi access points and routers to communicate and identify available networks and channels, enabling a more intelligent and adaptive channel load analysis algorithm that can optimize device association and channel selection. The proposed approach demonstrates a substantial increase in network throughput, with results showing that it outperforms existing solutions under both static and dynamic traffic conditions, culminating in a notable 52.3% improvement in the latter case.
